transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-18
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Lucas Patel (Redwood SE), Sanjay Rao (Opal SRE), Ellen Park (Opal ML), Tomás Ortega (Opal CTO)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on streaming generation p95 targets, concurrency needs for live-chat use case, and whether Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private best fits Opal's latency SLAs and cost envelope. Agreed to run an isolated streaming benchmark with their 10 canonical prompts.

Topics covered:
- p50/p95/p99 latency objectives for streaming generation
- concurrency shaping (connections / clients) and token/sec throughput expectations
- KV cache warm vs cold behavior and prefix caching for conversational use
- quantization/FP16 impact on p95 and tail latency
- fallback routing (hosted->dedicated) and autoscale burst policies
- security: VPC private control plane vs Hosted data retention concerns
\Action items: see metadata above
\Transcript body:
00:00:02 Maya Chen: okay, hey everyone, thanks for making time. this is Maya from Redwood, and I brought Lucas on who's our SE lead for throughput and streaming. how's everyone doing?
00:00:08 Tomás Ortega: good, thanks. excited to get into the numbers. we have a hard sla so want concrete p95s.
00:00:14 Maya Chen: yeah exactly, can you start with what target p95 you're aiming for and at what concurrency?
00:00:21 Tomás Ortega: we're aiming for p95 under 300ms for first token on short responses, and for streaming steady state we'd like token throughput around 200 tokens/sec per client at bursts up to 1k concurrent connections overall.
00:00:35 Sanjay Rao: just to add, our production will have about 400-700 active chatting users normally, peaks at 1,000. typical prompt length is 30-80 tokens but responses can be up to 800 tokens for long form.
00:00:48 Lucas Patel: cool. couple clarifying q's — when you say p95 under 300ms for first token is that cold start, warmed model with KV cache, or peering warm state?
00:00:57 Ellen Park: that is for warmed state. cold starts are allowed to be higher, but can't be more than 1.5s.
00:01:03 Lucas Patel: got it. so our streaming paths typically look different for first token vs subsequent tokens — first token often impacted by decoding and kernel dispatch. are you planning hosted or private?
00:01:13 Tomás Ortega: we'd prefer hosted for speed of rollout but need more SLA confidence. dedicated's interesting if it gives more predictable p95 tails.
00:01:20 Maya Chen: yep, that's the common tradeoff. Hosted gives fastest onboarding but multi-tenant variance can nudge the tail. Dedicated gives more predictable latency because of reserved pools and pinned capacity, and Private (VPC/on-prem) is for customers needing network isolation and customer-managed KMS.
00:01:34 Sanjay Rao: what about streaming—do you do chunked transmission or server-sent events? we need sub-100ms between token chunks to feel real-time.
00:01:42 Lucas Patel: Redwood supports chunked streaming via SSE and HTTP/2 streaming. The inter-token latency depends on model size, batching, and tokenization. for smaller models and quantized configs we can hit sub-50ms inter-token for short sequences, but for 8k context models it's higher. also, batching strategy matters — continuous batching can add 10-40ms at p95 if not tuned.
00:01:59 Ellen Park: you mentioned continuous batching — can that be tuned per-route? we have a mix of chat and summarize endpoints.
00:02:05 Lucas Patel: yes, batching parameters are per-model and per-route. you can set max-latency, preferred batch size, and also have a streaming-aware lower-latency path that sacrifices throughput. we usually recommend different profiles for chat (low-latency) vs batch summarization (optimise throughput).
00:02:20 Tomás Ortega: and the KV cache — does the cache live on gpu, and how warm is it after n requests?
00:02:26 Lucas Patel: KV cache is in-GPU or pinned fast memory depending on deployment. for conversation workloads, after 1-2 tokens it's warmed and subsequent tokens avoid recomputing the full attention. in our tests, prefix caching cut p95 for continuing conversations by ~30-50% compared to cold prompts.
00:02:41 Sanjay Rao: what's the behavior when we scale from 200 to 1k concurrent? do you shard the GPU state or spin up more instances?
00:02:47 Lucas Patel: autoscaling will spin up additional workers. with Dedicated you get reserved nurseries —we call them GPU pools— with burst policy. worst-case tail depends on how quickly autoscale reacts and how much reserved capacity you hold. if you need hard p95 targets under spikes, we recommend reserved capacity sized for peak or a hybrid reserved + burst policy.
00:03:04 Ellen Park: price impact on reserved peak? curious on example numbers.
00:03:07 Maya Chen: we'll send a pricing example but ballpark — Dedicated with reserved capacity is more cost predictable; Hosted can be cheaper for steady low throughput. we'll include concrete cost per 1M tokens for the prompt/response sizes you shared.
00:03:17 Tomás Ortega: can you run streaming benchmarks with our prompt set? we'd like to see end-to-end p95 and tokens/sec across client counts.
00:03:23 Lucas Patel: yes. ideal is an isolated benchmark with a Redwood ephemeral test account using your prompts and a traffic trace. Lucas: i'll prepare a harness that reproduces your inter-arrival times, connection churn, and sequence lengths.
00:03:33 Sanjay Rao: one more — fallback routing. if a hosted node is overloaded do you have automatic fallback to a cheaper model or different region?
00:03:40 Lucas Patel: we have smart routing policies. you can set policy: prefer host-region, then fallback to dedicated variant or smaller quantized model. fallback can be automatic with percent-based failover, or manual. we also support canary rollouts and automatic downgrade to a lower-latency quantized profile if quality thresholds pass.
00:03:56 Ellen Park: quality regressions are a concern. how do you guard against hallucination/regression when using quantized fallbacks?
00:04:03 Lucas Patel: our Optimize tooling runs quality checks against prompt eval sets; you can set regression thresholds. if quantization introduces unacceptable regressions, the runtime will avoid that fallback. we record per-generation quality metrics and tie them to alerts.
00:04:15 Tomás Ortega: network wise, our security folks want VPC + customer KMS. is that available for dedicated?
00:04:21 Maya Chen: yes, Dedicated supports VPC peering and Private (VPC/on-prem) offers a customer-managed control plane; you can also bring your own KMS. we'll provide SOC2/ISO docs.
00:04:30 Sanjay Rao: great. about metrics — we need token-level breakdowns and per-route p95s for cost attribution.
00:04:36 Lucas Patel: Redwood Console gives token-level cost, per-route latency histograms, and tracing hooks. we also export raw traces for your observability stack.
00:04:43 Ellen Park: can you run a benchmark that measures cold start percentiles? we need to understand cold vs warm tails for 99%ile.
00:04:49 Lucas Patel: yes, we'll instrument cold-start windows and report p50/p95/p99 for both first-token and streaming inter-token rates. in our internal tests cold-start p95 for a 13B model on dedicated was ~800-1,200ms depending on quantization; warming and warm-KV cache drops that substantially.
00:05:05 Tomás Ortega: do you support kernel selection tuned for sequence length? we've seen weird regressions when a kernel picks a less optimal matmul path for 1k sequences.
00:05:11 Lucas Patel: our compilation layer profiles sequence length distributions and picks kernels accordingly; we can also pin a kernel set per deployment if needed to avoid surprises.
00:05:19 Maya Chen: ok, i want to ask about pass-through load — can you simulate client-side backpressure? we sometimes have long poll clients that accumulate tokens.
00:05:26 Lucas Patel: yes, the test harness will support backpressure patterns and long-polled connections. we can simulate clients reading at different rates to measure how per-connection buffering affects server memory and latency.
00:05:36 Sanjay Rao: what about telemetry overhead — does tracing add visible latency in streaming?
00:05:40 Lucas Patel: tracing hooks are async; minimal impact on p95 but we'll run with tracing enabled during a benchmark to quantify.
00:05:46 Ellen Park: any gotchas with tokenization differences? we saw 10% token count delta between tokenizers.
00:05:50 Lucas Patel: yep, tokenizer differences change token/sec and cost. we'll use your tokenizer in the harness to match your production.
00:05:56 Tomás Ortega: ok let's recap next steps.
00:05:59 Maya Chen: sure — Lucas will ship the harness and config template, we'll get your 48h trace and prompt set, and schedule an isolated benchmark. I'll also send pricing and compliance docs.
00:06:07 Sanjay Rao: timeline OK. aiming to decide on Dedicated sizing by end of month.
00:06:10 Maya Chen: perfect. thanks all.
[End of recorded portion — remaining ~42 minutes were Q/A and deep dive logs captured below with timestamps]

00:06:45 Lucas Patel: deep dive: sample benchmarking plan — step 1: baseline using current opal prompts on Redwood Hosted smallest latency profile; step 2: run dedicated pool with 2 GPU nodes, observe p95 at 100/400/1000 concurrent; step 3: run quantized profile (4-bit) to check tail; step 4: run cold-start window test (connections reopened every Xs) ; step 5: analyze token/sec and per-route cost.
00:07:12 Sanjay Rao: do you have historical numbers for tail when guests are multi-tenant? we need to budget for noise.
00:07:17 Lucas Patel: multi-tenant noise at p95 varies but we've seen hosted p95 tails 1.1x-1.8x compared to reserved for same workload. depends on burstiness.
00:07:25 Ellen Park: when you say 4-bit quantization — any memory/regress tradeoffs?
00:07:28 Lucas Patel: 4-bit gains on memory and throughput but can introduce small quality diffs; that's why we run evals and automatic rollback. for some LLM families 4-bit is near-lossless for conversational tasks.
00:07:40 Tomás Ortega: curious about throttling — can Redwood do per-customer rate-limits at token-level to avoid noisy neighbors?
00:07:46 Maya Chen: yes, rate limits and token quotas are configurable per-token and per-route; and you can reserve capacity for high-tier customers.
00:07:53 Sanjay Rao: one practical question — our security team requires an audit log of model input/outputs for 90 days. does Redwood provide that?
00:07:59 Maya Chen: yes we can retain logs; with Private you can keep logs in your S3, otherwise Redwood Hosted offers configurable retention windows. we can surface those logs in Console or export them.
00:08:08 Ellen Park: about p99 — our ops lead wants p99 < 1s for interactive sessions. is that realistic?
00:08:14 Lucas Patel: p99 < 1s for warmed streaming short-responses is achievable on Dedicated with proper sizing and reserved burst. for long-form responses p99 will be dominated by generation time and can exceed that depending on token count.
00:08:25 Tomás Ortega: any latency regression risk when adding more routes? we have dozens of microservices hitting the model.
00:08:30 Lucas Patel: per-route isolation and quotas help; Dedicated pools can be split by route to prevent cross-traffic interference.
00:08:37 Sanjay Rao: ok what about observability hooks — will we get per-token timings exported to datadog?
00:08:42 Lucas Patel: yes we have exporters for Datadog, Prometheus, and can stream traces to your APM.
00:08:48 Ellen Park: any special considerations for GPU packing? we care about CUDA kernels and fragmentation when several midsize jobs run.
00:08:54 Lucas Patel: runtime does GPU packing aware of memory footprints; for predictable tails we recommend Dedicated pinned instances instead of aggressive packing.
00:09:03 Maya Chen: quick note — i'll drop the SOC2 + ISO docs in the shared folder after the call.
00:09:08 Tomás Ortega: thanks.
00:09:18 Lucas Patel: benchmark specifics i will include: - traffic replay tool - prompt set - seed for RNGs - measurement for first-token and inter-token - measurement for cold vs warm - kernel/profile dumps - KV cache hit rates - per-route token cost
00:09:35 Sanjay Rao: and include the model versions you'll run and exact quant params.
00:09:39 Lucas Patel: will do.
00:09:46 Maya Chen: any more Qs?
00:09:50 Tomás Ortega: one more on data residency — do you have eu-only hosting?
00:09:55 Maya Chen: yes, Redwood has EU regions and we can pin deployment to EU-only for data residency. Private on-prem also possible if required.
00:10:03 Ellen Park: okay that's all for me.
00:10:06 Sanjay Rao: good. thanks for walking through.
00:10:10 Maya Chen: great, we'll follow up with the harness and schedule. thanks everyone.
